fatal_errors: The proposed coarser 30–75 μm feedstock is not the demonstrated intervention; the target used fine 5–30 μm powder and optimized a low-temperature ID-HVAF-i7 operating condition to produce an approximately 150 μm coating.

The hypothesis assumes that greater particle mass will increase coating thickness under otherwise unchanged spray parameters, but coarser particles can be insufficiently heated or accelerated and may instead reduce deposition efficiency and cohesion.
Neither cited source demonstrates that changing FeCoNiCrAl feedstock from 15–45 μm to 30–75 μm increases attainable thickness while preserving low oxidation.
Operating and service conditions are not specified quantitatively, omitting the relevant substrate preheat and the demonstrated 1000–1150 °C, 50 h isothermal exposure boundary.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses the stated thickness/oxidation tradeoff and proposes a single, testable intervention, but it does not reconstruct the supported process solution. The target result arose from optimized medium-pressure, low-temperature ID-HVAF-i7 spraying, which achieved 79% deposition efficiency, 0.2% porosity, retained BCC structure, and an approximately 150 μm coating. The proposed particle-size mechanism is only generally plausible and overlooks incomplete melting and reduced impact velocity for coarse particles. Its evidence discusses in-flight oxidation and splat morphology but does not support the claimed size-dependent thickness improvement. The controlled comparison and explicit falsification threshold are useful, although oxidation should be quantified more sensitively than by XRD alone and service oxidation/TGO behavior should also be tested.
